Doom 1 was an extraordinary FPS. The pacing and mechanical minutiae are still fresh today, even though some may find a lot of it outdated. I know millenials who, despite their initial hesitation, outright claim that the Brutal Doom mod is the greatest FPS they've ever played. For the most part, original Doom a decisively nuclear shooting experience by not suffering from modern ballast like story, cover mechanics, meta-systems like upgrading, complex puzzles or environment interaction etc ( - all of which can work in their own right)

Another factor of success was the horror scifi setting. It framed an outworldly canvas of carnage and bitter struggle. The doomguy was literally fighting and marching through hell, and he was knee deep in the dead. Its always easy in retrospect to see that something works or not, but another setting, say, WW2 would have been so much worse.

Doom 3 kept the setting and feel but changed the mechanics. The facelift was no easy task as most games from 2004 aged terribly. Doom 1's setting featured a plethora of spaceport hallways and spiky hellholes. Could such an eclectic style, which helped to make Doom 1 & 2 a fantastic experience, transition to a more photorealistic 3d? Thankfully, normal maps and real time shadows were just becoming technically feasible. While certainly more conservative, the atmosphere was solid. So what about the mechanics? With no pseudo 2d, the constraints of an established genre it helped to birth were tested and tried by hundreds of iterations. The press was clear, Half Life 2, which came three months later, was the best shooter of 2004, mostly thanks to Alyx, the Gravity Gun and a large, interestingly designed world. But I say: HL was the better gaming spectacle -nothing wrong with that- but Doom 3 was clearly the better FPS.

A great game is, among other things, characterized by the ability to master it. In this regard, Doom 3 is a rare jewel among AAA FPS. The whole carnage is extremely fair, once you get to know the monsters, you can overcome nearly all situations just by skill and emerge unscathed. Not so in HL, where skill is much more tied to the knowledge of where something will pop up- which is why HL is the spiritual ancestor to modern FPS.
Doom got this right by not giving most monsters guns. Instead, they grab, punch, gore or throw fireballs at you. Everything is foreseeable, dodgeable, adjustable. You manage split seconds and are rewarded with clean victories, while in HL, you manage health and ammo to be rewarded more health and ammo.

Doom 4, really the third game in the series, again, faces the harsh pressure of high expectation. With a retarded press ( check this noob out ), the whole process today is more about creating a bunch of hyperexcited drones that push your spectacle. That's why every game journalist harps about how "that is doom, that is sooo like doom is supposed to be" even when the game looks like Quake 3 or Unreal Tournament or maybe rather like the Xenomorph from Alien 3 - a camera gliding at high speed towards the enemy in order to devour him. This is not doom esthetically, remember, demons were supposedly trying to eat the player, who was trying to escape hell, not assault it. Is this a clever pun about the invasion of Europe? Because it feels like those emaciated Imps, clearly the token trans characters du jour, desperately try to protect their turf from a merciless foreign intruder. And what about the shooty parts? Is it more like Doom 1, where hordes of enemies were trying to overwhelm you in these corridors? Or more like Doom 3, where finding the ideal path of dodging and emptying the shotgun in a split-second meant all the difference? No, Doom 4 seems more like ... fucking Serious Sam: You move into a boxy area, where you now have to kill every dude for the doors to magically open. But hey, there's also coloured keycards if you're into FPS oldschool missionary doorplay. The weird melee executions, which the game heavily rewards, changes everything into a high paced melee. Like in a PvE Multiplayer, you move forward. Doom 1 & 3 threw monsters at you trying to overwhelm you, now you overwhelm the monsters.

That is so not Doom.

Not sure if the OP is joking or not. I was a major skeptic about Doom 4. I've been playing DOOM 1 & 2 since they were released, and I've had them on every single computer I've ever owned. I hated Doom 3; it wasn't anything like the originals--I know it has some fans, but between cut scenes and game mechanics that required you to HIDE, I was just put-off.

After playing the horrible multi-player demo a couple of weeks ago, I was pretty much disgusted. However, I saw that Kinguin was selling Doom 4 keys at about half-off, so I decided to pick one up. I justified this because I am an OG DOOM player, and if I plunked down the $ for Duke Nukem Forever, I figured I should for this too. I have to admit I've been very surprised at the SP mode. It is solid. Does it capture the spirit of the original DOOM? No--at least not as much as I'd like. But it is a solid run & gun shooter. I like the fact that it plays up the "hell" elements. I'm not very keen on the outdoor combat in the early levels--DOOM's early levels were primarily set indoors. The jumping doesn't bother me although I thought I'd hate it.

The most authentic thing about Doom 4? It runs for shit on my i7 w/16gb of ram! My GPU is old, but nothing I've played (for years) has had a problem--until now. It's like I've been transported back to the 90s when every new id game required a video card upgrade. I had to lower my resolution to 720p and dial back all the graphics settings to "low" to get a playable framerate.

That aside, the SP game is good and worth buying. And that's coming from a dude who was extremely skeptical. If Bethesda actually allows it to be modded, it could potentially be great--but only time will tell. Is it as good as DOOM I & II? No. Is it as good as Serious Sam HD (which I consider the modern gold-standard of the run & gun genre)? No. Is it as good as other modern FPSs? Yes--and probably better than most.
It's a terrible Doom game. It's a decent to above average FPS game. That's where I sit.

I wouldn't disagree with you completely. It reminds me MUCH more of Quake II more than DOOM. They really blew an opportunity to DOOM-ify it by choosing to go with a muted color pallate. For the life of me, I don't understand why they made that decision--if they had used the original color scheme, it would have at least given the new game a visual similarity to the original.

That said, they do get a few things right. Movement is good and harkens back to the original. The jump/double-jump is a somewhat questionable choice, but it works. It should be noted that the original DOOM was 2.5D so jumping (or mouselook) wasn't necessary whereas in true 3D engines it is sort of a requirement.

The "glory kills" are a bit over the top and derivative of Brutal Doom, but they've incorporated them pretty well. I hear you can turn them off, but I haven't tried.

As someone who follows the DOOM speedrunning community, I appreciate the fast-action in the new game. If someone can create map packs as good as the old Memento Mori the new version will have legs--but it remains to be seen how "open" Bethesda will be.

But all-in-all you're right--the new game is more like a distant-cousin to DOOM I & II. I would have much preferred if Croteam had been given the chance to develop Doom 4; they are the only studio that has fully captured the original's gameplay in a modern context.

I think games nowadays have a tough time meeting the mechanics and feel of those old school games because of how these games also try to match real world physics and pacing. 3D gaming pushed developers to achieve the most realistic, immersive experience possible. While Doom 4 does an incredible job of making a hellish atmosphere, it's never going to hit the nail on the timed strafing and almost choreographed style of the originals.

Take a look at Hotline Miami. It's sort of the same idea. The fact that it's not trying to be realistic means they can use simple mechanics to make the gameplay feel like a dance, where all the movements have to be perfect and well-executed.

It's the Final Fantasy XIII gambit that SE faced a few years back.

People want old school gameplay with modern visuals, but the modern visuals are almost wasted on old school gameplay.

Dooms glory was theme and level design. If they fail at even one of those it's suddenly not Doom. The theme from what I've seen seems spot on, but the level designs as people have pointed out are more Halo. Which might work if the gameplay had remained more basic and true to the founding games.

I can't hate on the developers for it at all because it has to have some blend of modern and classic for mass appeal to sell, but if theme is the only tie in you'll alienate the old school fans who are the bread and butter foundation of your sales.
